blocks.prompt: The Mermaid That Was Really a Sea Cow
blocks.text: Mermaids are not real. But sailors used to think they were. Long ago, ships spent months at sea. The sailors were tired and far from home. Sometimes they saw a big animal lift its head out of the water. It had a round face. It held its baby with one flipper. From far away, in the fog, it looked a little like a person. So the sailors called it a mermaid. It was really a manatee, a slow and gentle sea animal. A manatee is not fancy like the mermaids in stories. But it is real, and it is kind.

blocks.prompt: The Mermaids Columbus Saw
blocks.text: In the year 1493, a sailor named Christopher Columbus was sailing near the islands of the Caribbean. One morning he wrote something strange in his journal. He said he had seen three mermaids rise up out of the sea. But Columbus was not impressed. He wrote that they were not as beautiful as people say. He thought real mermaids should be prettier. So what did Columbus really see? Almost certainly, he saw manatees. A manatee is a large, slow sea animal with a round tail and a whiskered face. It comes up to the surface to breathe. It can lift the top of its body out of the water. To a tired sailor who had been at sea for weeks, a manatee bobbing in the waves might look like a person with a fish tail. Columbus was not lying and he was not silly. He simply saw a real animal he did not know, and he reached for the closest word he had. That word was mermaid.

blocks.prompt: Why Half a Fish?
blocks.text: Mermaid stories are older than almost any story we still tell. Ancient people who lived by the sea told of women who lived in the water. The Greeks sang of sirens, and the people of Syria honored a goddess who was said to be part fish. Wherever people lived close to the ocean, some version of the half-human, half-fish idea seemed to appear. Why a fish tail? Think about what the sea meant to people long ago. It fed them and it frightened them. It could be calm one day and sink a whole ship the next. A creature that was half like us and half like the deep water was a way to picture that mix of beauty and danger in one body. There is a real animal tangled up in the legend. When scientists sorted the animal world into groups, they gave a special name to the family that includes manatees and dugongs. They called it Sirenia, after the sirens of the old sea stories. The name is a quiet joke and a clue at the same time. It admits that these gentle, plant-eating sea animals are probably the creatures sailors mistook for mermaids for hundreds of years. A dugong is the best example. It lives in warm, shallow seas, it has a broad tail shaped like a paddle, and a mother dugong will hold her calf as she rises to breathe. Seen from a rocking ship, in poor light, by someone who wanted to see something, a dugong could become a mermaid in an instant. The legend and the animal have been swimming together for a very long time.

blocks.prompt: The Beautiful Lie and the Gentle Truth
blocks.text: For most of human history, educated people believed mermaids were real. This is easy to forget. We file mermaids next to fairies and unicorns, but for centuries they sat in a different drawer, alongside animals that had simply not been listed yet. Sailors reported them. Mapmakers drew them. In 1493, Christopher Columbus recorded in his log that he had seen three mermaids off the coast of the Caribbean, adding, with a note of disappointment, that they were not as beautiful as they are painted. He was almost certainly looking at manatees. That single line explains a great deal. Columbus did not think he was inventing anything. He believed mermaids existed, so when a strange animal lifted its face out of the water, mermaid was a reasonable label. The gap between the legend and the animal was filled by expectation. People saw what they already believed was there. Two forces kept the belief alive. The first was loneliness. A voyage could last months, the crew exhausted and homesick, the sea endlessly the same. A mind in that state is generous with what it sees. The second force was profit. In 1842, the showman P. T. Barnum exhibited what he called the Feejee Mermaid, and crowds paid to see it. It was a fake, the dried upper body of a monkey stitched to the tail of a fish, shriveled and ugly. People came anyway, because they wanted the creature to be real. Slowly, the mermaid changed jobs. As science identified the manatees and dugongs and grouped them under the name Sirenia, in honor of the sirens, the mermaid lost her place among real animals. She did not disappear. She moved into art. In 1837, the Danish writer Hans Christian Andersen published The Little Mermaid, a story not about a monster or a sailor's mistake, but about longing and sacrifice. The statue built for that story now sits in the harbor at Copenhagen, and people travel across the world to photograph it. That is the strange arc of the mermaid. She began as an honest error, a real animal seen through tired eyes and hopeful minds. She survived because people wanted her to. And when the ocean finally gave up its secret, she changed from a fact into a feeling, which turned out to be a much safer place to live.

blocks.prompt: The Creature We Invented Twice
blocks.text: The mermaid is a creature we invented twice. The first invention was a mistake, and the second was a choice, and the distance between them is the whole story. Begin with the mistake. For thousands of years, people who lived by the sea told of women who lived in the water. The oldest versions are not quite mermaids as we picture them. In Homer's Odyssey, written nearly three thousand years ago, the sirens who lure sailors to their deaths are part bird, not part fish. Over the centuries, in the retelling, their feathers slowly turned to scales, and the bird woman of Greek song became the fish tailed woman of the sailor's tale. Ancient Syria told of Atargatis, a goddess pictured with the tail of a fish. The idea belonged to no single people. Wherever the ocean fed a community and occasionally drowned it, a half human shape seemed to rise out of the water in its stories. The reason is not hard to find, and it is swimming in warm, shallow seas right now. Manatees and dugongs are large, slow, air breathing mammals. A manatee surfaces to breathe with the top of its body lifted clear of the water. A dugong mother cradles her calf against her chest with a flipper as she rises. Their tails are broad and flat. Their faces, seen head on, are oddly expressive. To a sailor who had been months at sea, straining to see through spray and fog, and who already believed mermaids were real, one of these animals was not evidence of a myth. It was the myth, confirmed. In January of 1493, Christopher Columbus wrote in his journal that he had seen three mermaids near the coast of what is now the Dominican Republic. He was unimpressed, and complained that they were not as beautiful as they are painted. He was looking at manatees. Science eventually caught the joke and made it official. When naturalists organized the animal kingdom, they placed the manatees and dugongs in an order they named Sirenia, after the sirens of the old stories. The name is an admission carved into the record: these are the animals people mistook for mermaids. Here the story turns from error to invention. Once the ocean surrendered its secret, the mermaid should have died, the way belief in a flat sea died. She did not. She was too useful. In 1842, the showman P. T. Barnum drew paying crowds to the Feejee Mermaid, a grotesque fake sewn together from a monkey and a fish, and people came precisely because they wished it were true. Five years earlier, in 1837, the Danish writer Hans Christian Andersen had already shown where the mermaid would live next. His story The Little Mermaid was not about a sailor or a sea cow. It was about wanting a life you were not born into badly enough to give up your own voice for it. The mermaid had stopped being a claim about the world and become a claim about us. That is the second invention, and it is the durable one. As a fact, the mermaid was always going to lose, because manatees exist and mermaids do not. As a feeling, she cannot be disproved, because the longing she carries is real even though she is not. We built her first out of a misread animal and a hopeful eye. When that excuse ran out, we kept her anyway, and gave her the only job that could outlast the truth.
